title: 3-Read Friday #93
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 93 of 3-Read Friday moves from school culture to lesson structure to screens. Barton opens with Adam Boxer's piece on departmental autonomy, sharing his own experience that heads of department consistently want their teams to have autonomy while also wanting consistently good learning experiences for students -- a tension Barton says he has only found resolvable by removing autonomy in certain specific areas. He then turns to Dylan Kane's challenge to the I/we/you lesson structure, framing it as a genuine provocation given Barton's own fondness for that model, and summarising Kane's alternative of leaning on whole-class rapid-response methods like mini-whiteboards or student-generated problems to surface misunderstandings earlier. The issue closes with Jean Twenge's argument connecting the post-2012 decline in test scores to digital device use in schools -- not just smartphones, but school-issued laptops and tablets. Across the three items, Barton curates a mix of leadership philosophy, classroom-structure critique, and technology-and-attainment research.
points: Barton's own editorial addition to the Boxer piece is substantive, not just a pointer -- he states his own view that team autonomy is 'only achievable by removing autonomy in certain areas,' directly engaging with Boxer's autonomy-vs-anarchy distinction.

He frames Kane's I/we/you critique as a personal challenge, noting he is 'a big fan of that structure' -- signalling the issue is curating genuine disagreement rather than just work that confirms Barton's existing views.

Twenge's argument is summarised precisely: the test-score decline traces to 2012 and implicates school-issued devices specifically, not just personal smartphones -- a distinction Barton preserves rather than collapsing into a generic phone-ban narrative.

The issue's three items collectively move from leadership/culture, to classroom pedagogy, to a broader evidence-based critique of school technology policy -- a wider span than Barton's more tightly AI-focused recent issues.
quotes: Every head of department I have spoken to in the last 3 years says the same thing: I want my team to have autonomy… but I also want students to have a consistently good learning experience. I have found this is only achievable by removing autonomy in certain areas.
Dylan starts this post by saying: I’m not a fan of I/we/you lessons. Which is a challenge to me, because I am a big fan of that structure!

Dylan suggests that rather than leading everyone through a procedure first, leverage whole-class/Rapid-Response methods (like mini-whiteboards) or student-generated problems early to surface misunderstandings immediately.
Jean Twenge argues that declining student test scores, which began around 2012, are significantly linked to digital device use -- not just smartphones but school-issued laptops and tablets.
